lines: The first thing they took was my name.
Not with ceremony or proclamation. A shrug, and
an entry in a book.
I was Nagoji Sawant. Twenty-five. Huzurat
cavalry, household horse to Chimaji Appa, picked
out by sardars who had watched me ride.
Here I was a number.
Down here the hours
were kept by boots on
stone, and by the bucket
that carried away what
we left behind.
Above us, the bells rang for evening prayer.
Steady as monsoon rain on a Deccan roof.
Then Father Duarte came.
A holy man built for argument, not battle.
The calluses on his right hand said he had once
held something heavier than a quill.
Este. This one is stubborn.
He smelled of garlic sausage and chapel incense.
He was humming the hymn the bells had played.
Stubborn is better than broken. In any language.
How long since the last questioning?
Two days. He still insists he is only a horseman.
You understand our language, senhor marata?
Enough to know when I am being lied to, Father.
But you can speak your questions. I have heard
most of them already.
You see. He understands.
Bring him.
My joints had forgotten the shape of standing.
A Maratha horseman does not whimper in front of
an enemy. We bleed, we fall, we curse the gods
and get back up.
On the black soil of the
Deccan that had been
simple enough.
Here it took more effort.
The smell changed as we walked. Rotting straw
and waste gave way to oil, sweat, and something
sharp that stung the nose.
Wine and old fear.
This was where the Portuguese forged
information.
Nagoji Sawant. The Viceroy's spies insist you
were huzurat cavalry under Chimaji Appa himself.
What we do not
know is who
ordered the
attacks, how
many men you
had, and which
forts you meant
to strike next.
You know more than I do, then.
You have maps and books. You draw lines
on paper and call them borders.
My horse does not read.
Your horse is dead. We shot it when we brought
you in.
A pity. Fine animal.
Then he died better than I will.
Tell me this at least, Nagoji. Not for the Viceroy.
For me.
Do you believe you fight for God, for some higher
good, or is it simply for plunder and the honour of
your people?
For an instant the dungeon was gone, and I was
on a ridge above the Godavari, watching the dust
of a marching column.
I fight because I was born into a world where men
who do not fight are trampled.
As for God, Father, I leave Him to the Brahmins
and to you.
He seems to favour whoever has the
better powder.
You see. He gives you nothing. Let me loosen his
tongue.
The first wedge went under what remained of my
left thumbnail.
After that, pain lost its degrees.
Once you have felt your joints forced against the
way they were meant to bend, the mind floats
above the body and watches priests and gaolers
ply their trade.
Not yet.
The Viceroy needs a hand that can still hold a
quill.
Enough.
He still holds back names.
A dead prisoner cannot testify.
I closed my eyes. Not in prayer. In calculation.
How many guards. How often they changed. Which men wore keys and which carried only cudgels. How many steps from the stair to
the courtyard.
They are gathering us for transport. South. By
ship. For labour.
Ships meant movement. Movement meant
chances.
They had taken my name. They had tried to break
my body.
They had forgotten the simplest lesson of the
Deccan monsoon.
Storms do not ask permission.
